Item quæ de uerbis directis et communibus in tractatu substitutionum. hæc sunt Lunæ uersatilis incommoda, quæ cum noctis tenebras pellere debeat, ut tu dixisti in §. j. ut iudic. fin. quo. col. ij. licet parum ad rem, maiores tenebras conduplicat. Videbor ego tibi Stoam inuadere, Academiam incendere, Peripatum demoliri, si à Bart. dissentiam uel à communi aliorum opinione. Cæterum non possum assentiri Bartolo, qui olim donationem contractum nominatum fuisse existimat, hodie quoque multomagis esse, neque reliquis interpretibus, qui hodie quidem nominatum esse uolunt, olim uerò non, sed, quod mireris, etiam post l. siquis argentum. §. fi. C. de dona. innominatam donationem assero.

Obiicit Bart. l. Aristo. ff. de don. ubi in donatione non est locus pœnitentiæ: in contractibus innominatis est l. si pecuniam. de cond. ob caus. ff. Cui uulgo respondetur, nullam conuentionem innominatam non reciprocam post traditionem pœnitentiam recipere, & uerum est.

Idem Barto. falsò notat donationem habere nomen ab executione, & à re tradita exemplo mutui, commodati, depositi, quia donatio est doni datio. l. senatus de don. cau. ff. idcirco, inquit, nisi re ipsa non producit actionem, quamuis nomen elegans habebat. Sed donationem fuisse ante traditionem demonstrat d. l. siquis argentum. §. fi. C. de donat. ibi, ut non inutilis. ut de permutatione dici solet. Prorsus autem innominatam esse probo his ratiunculis, quia neque nomen suum habet, neque actionem. In tantum enim late patet, ut stipulationem sine causa factam contineat. l. hoc iure. §. fi. ff. de donat. Actione uerò deficit, quia nusquam est actio. nam quæ actio in d. §. fi. l. si quis argentum pro donatione competit, ex lege uocatur. ex eo enim quòd actio ex lege datur, donatio per se imbecilla ostenditur. l. j. ff. de codic. ex leg. &, ut Luna, alieno lumine lucet, cum careat proprio. Digest 9.2.27. **MOM.** The Moon is argued for its inconstancy in a miraculous way; for it is sometimes whole, sometimes half, waxing, waning, silent, curved with horns. And for this reason the Doctors are poorly regarded, because they feel, disagree, distinguish, and divide things into a thousand atoms, not without great cost to the readers. And so, just as those conceived under the Moon fall into the falling sickness, as Quintus Serenus is the author, and those who spend a long time under the Moon fall into delirium, and are called "lunatics" by the jurist in Digest 21.1.1.8, so for the most part, those who follow the trifles and empty disputations of the Doctors everywhere fall into total folly, as those which were invented concerning the "extremes from which" and "extremes to which" in Digest 41.3.31. Likewise, those things concerning direct and common words in the treatise on substitutions. These are the inconveniences of the changeable Moon, which, although it ought to dispel the darkness of the night, as you said in the authentication *Ut iudicia*, section 2, column 2, it doubles the greater darkness, even if it has little to do with the matter. I will seem to you to invade the Stoa, to burn down the Academy, to demolish the Peripatetic school, if I disagree with Bartolus or with the common opinion of others. However, I cannot agree with Bartolus, who thinks that a donation was once a named contract, and is even much more so today, nor with the remaining interpreters, who indeed wish it to be named today, but not formerly, but, what you might wonder at, I assert even after Code 8.53.35 that a donation is an unnamed contract.

Bartolus objects to Digest 39.5.1, where in a donation there is no place for repentance; in unnamed contracts there is, Digest 12.4.3. To which it is commonly responded that no unnamed convention that is not reciprocal admits of repentance after tradition, and it is true.

The same Bartolus falsely notes that a donation takes its name from execution and from the thing handed over, by the example of a loan, a bailment, and a deposit, because a donation is a "giving of a gift," Digest 39.5.1. Therefore, he says, unless it is by the thing itself, it does not produce an action, although it had an elegant name. But that a donation existed before tradition is demonstrated by the said Code 8.53.35, "that it not be useless," as is wont to be said about permutation. I prove that it is entirely unnamed by these little reasons: because it has neither its own name, nor its own action. For it lies so wide that it contains a stipulation made without cause, Digest 39.5.1. But it lacks an action, because there is nowhere an action. For what action competes for a donation in the said section 5 of the law *Si quis argentum*, it is called by law. For from the fact that an action is given by law, the donation itself is shown to be weak, Digest 28.2.29, and, like the Moon, it shines with borrowed light, since it lacks its own. bit: *Animalitas conversa ad rationem, quae mater est vivorum, id est bonorum operum, vel recte factorum, quibus contraria sunt peccata, quae dicuntur mortua. Verum haec longius petita sunt, neque Spiritus Sanctus hic per Adamum inordinate procedere, vel ordinem invertere voluit: nam Vita bonorum operum necessario Vitam fidei, vel Vitam in Messia praesupponit, et ante se requirit: haec autem in Messia fundata Vita spiritualis hic in contextu paginam utramque facit. Breviter haec explicatio de Vita Morali non sensum, sed usum, non immediatam, et proximam explicationem, sed mediatam, et remotam applicationem attendit.*

14. Aliis placet *sensus Verborum Politicus, vel Oeconomicus, quod Adamus in hac Onomathesia virilem autoritatem, et potestatem, in uxorem ostendere voluerit, nimirum quod maritalis sit dignitatis, vel autoritatis, facultatis, vel potestatis, juris, et regiminis, Uxori nomen imponere, cum alias Uxores in Maritorum Nomen, et Familiam, potestatem, atque dominationem transeant, non contra. Verum Adamus hic nihil de sua vel dignitate, vel autoritate, nihil de jure, vel potestate, nihil de regimine, vel dominio, cogitabat, neque sua, sed ea, quae per divinam informationem audiverat, cogitabat, non suam, sed Messiae gloriam spectabat, et majora, meliora, sublimiora, sicut edoctus erat, resonabat. Qualis fuerat Dei sermo, talis etiam Adami dicitur Echo. Vitam spiritualem Deus sonabat, et Spiritus Sanctus eidem insonabat, Vitam spiritualem etiam Adami lingua resonabat.*

15. His igitur praesuppositis, nunc Compendium Adami Theologicum clarius conspicimus: tum quia *Vita spiritualis*, et *caelestis* est finis omnium articulorum fidei, vel Dogmatum Theologiae, cum *fidei finis sit salus, seu vera vita*: 1. Petri I. 9. tum quia Vita Spiritualis est *nucleus*, circa quem servandum, et ad usum applicandum, tota Theologia versatur: tum quia *Vita spiritualis* est centrum universae Theologiae, dum omnes lineae *Doctrinales* Theologiae partium ex hoc centro fluunt, et ad illud unice respiciunt: tum quia *vita spiritualis, vita mystica* Theologiae, per quam omnia capita Theologica vere vivificantur: est *anima Theologiae*, per quam omnes Theologiae partes nobis animantur.

<vocab>Animalitas, Onomathesia, Messia, Vita spiritualis, Compendium Adami, Dogmatum Theologiae, vita mystica, anima Theologiae</vocab>
translation:
Animal life turned toward reason, which is the mother of the living, that is, of good works, or of rightly performed deeds, to which are contrary those sins which are called dead. Truly, these things are sought from afar, nor did the Holy Spirit wish for Adam to proceed here in a disorderly manner, or to invert the order: for the life of good works necessarily presupposes, and requires before it, the life of faith, or the life in the Messiah; however, this spiritual life, founded in the Messiah, brings about both pages here in the context. Briefly, this explanation concerning moral life looks not to the sense, but to the use, not to the immediate and proximate explanation, but to the mediate and remote application.

14. To others, the political or economic sense of the words is pleasing, that Adam in this naming wished to show manly authority and power over his wife, namely that it is a matter of marital dignity, or authority, faculty, or power, right, and governance, to impose a name upon a wife, whereas otherwise wives pass into the name, family, power, and dominion of husbands, not the contrary. But Adam thought nothing here of his own dignity or authority, nothing of right or power, nothing of governance or dominion, and he did not ponder his own things, but those which he had heard through divine information; he was not looking to his own glory, but to the glory of the Messiah, and he was echoing greater, better, and more sublime things, just as he had been taught. Such as the Word of God had been, such also is the Echo of Adam said to be. God sounded forth spiritual life, and the Holy Spirit sounded it into him; the tongue of Adam also echoed forth spiritual life.

15. With these things therefore presupposed, we now see the Theological Compendium of Adam more clearly: both because spiritual and heavenly life is the end of all articles of faith, or dogmas of theology, since the end of faith is salvation, or true life (1 Peter 1:9); and because spiritual life is the nucleus around which all theology revolves, to be preserved and applied to use; and because spiritual life is the center of universal theology, while all the doctrinal lines of the parts of theology flow from this center and look solely to it; and because spiritual life, the mystical life of theology, through which all theological chapters are truly vivified, is the soul of theology, through which all parts of theology are animated for us.

The first is called apparent, which is in the cognition of future things that can be known beforehand from these causes. Thus, a physician knows health or death beforehand. There is an order to such effects in knowing in some causes.

The second is prophecy improperly spoken, which communicates to someone prone to prophecy without such intelligence, according to what is held in Daniel 6: "There is need of intelligence in the vision." Jerome holds this same view in the beginning of his commentary on Isaiah. It happens that this occurs in three ways. In one way in a vision, thus Pharaoh saw ears of corn in a general way, and Belshazzar saw a hand writing on the wall (Daniel 7). The former was sleeping, the latter waking, yet neither of them was a prophet. But Daniel and Joseph, who understood the visions, were. Secondly, it happens in speech; thus Caiaphas (John 11) said a prophetic word, intending only to give counsel about the death of Christ, that it would be expedient, although he was innocent, lest the Romans come and take away their place and nation because of him. But this counsel was brought about by the Holy Spirit. He thus uttered that the death of Christ would be for the spiritual salvation of the whole world, while Caiaphas himself was ignorant of this; he was a rational animal, although through his tongue a rational word was uttered by an angel moving his tongue, without him knowing. Thirdly, this happens in operation, when the spirit moves someone to do something which has an outcome by itself, although the man moved is ignorant of the end; thus Judges 11 says of Jephthah that "the spirit of the Lord rushed upon him" to fight against the sons of Ammon, although future victory was not revealed to him. And such a motion is called the instinct of the Holy Spirit, which is a falling short of the definition of prophecy, according to the doctors, and such a motion is similar to the motion of the fortunate who moves toward something good without reason and prior knowledge, as is held in the book <term>On Good Fortune</term>. It differs, however, that the motion of the fortunate is from a natural cause, namely, from the influence of the heavens or the intelligence of the mover, as some say, or from both together, as others say. But the motion of Jephthah and Caiaphas is from a supernatural cause, namely, from the motion of the divine Spirit. This instinct approaches more closely to the definition of prophecy than the other two modes proposed. The third is prophecy true and properly spoken, which is understood as prophecy that is also found in a multiple degree, of which one is more excellent than the other; hence, for the rest, there is clearer intelligence. The first degree of this prophecy is that which, when communicated with a vision, is given with the intelligence of the vision; thus Jeremiah sees a burning pot and its face from the face of the north (Jeremiah 1), and he understood and this was signified as the army of the king of Babylon about to come to burn the city of Jerusalem.
The second degree, which is not such a vision or appearance, but hearing a voice instructing about something supernatural. 1 Kings 3: Samuel heard the voice of the Lord speaking, and yet he did not see any figure appearing to him.

Further you must know the names of the pieces and of the places: for the Chesse men that are on the kings side, be named the Kings Chesse men, and likewise the kings houses unto the middest of the Chesse boorde. And from thence forward are the contrary kings houses. As for example: The Pawne which is before thy king, is in the second house of thy king. And if thou remove him one step, he shall be in the third, or if he go further, in the fourth house of the king: But afterwards and if he doe goe further yet, hee shall be in the fourth house of the King of the contrary parte. And so of all the other Chesse men on that side. The other side is that of the Queene, as well in Chesse men, as in houses, therefore for this cause is it needful to have before you a Chesse boorde with the Chesse men, for to see with your eyes the Arte which briefly shall be declared in this Treatise. And so, after presupposing the game, you may beginne after two sortes to play it as followeth.

### The first maner of playing.

The first manner is to beginne with the Kings Pawne: and the second is to begin with the Queens Pawne. The first (according to my judgement) is the best: that is to wit, to beginne with the Kings Pawne as farre as he may goe. Ecclesiæ: Et (a.) parte superstes vivit suis in filijs (quos Christo genuit) profuso lacte animat ad constantiam, stimulat in pugnam, solidat ad victoriam, componit ad triumphos. O fœcunditatem felicissimam coronatæ Laurûs CATHARINÆ, quæ tot beata fructibus arbor fæcundos sequacium germinum traduces posteritati transmisit. Arborem vitæ dixeris hanc Laurum, cujus immortalis vigor in flore mortali, feracium adhuc florum spem viridem ostentans, à sæculis egressus in sæcula progreditur, nec temporis vetustate venustatem, nec hostilium procellarum turbine virorem amissurus, per ipsa florum funera vitam immortalem negotiatur : Fructus sui morsum indulsit sanguinis Helluoni Maximino, ut voracem ejus ingluviem satiaret. Maximini ferro primos dimittit surculos, ut per succisa Martyrum germina, cælestibus hortis inferatur. Lacte manat & purpurâ, ut mori non erubescat, aut certè dulciùs se mori ostendat (dulcissimum enim est mori triumphantem) quàm Tyrannus vivat. Vernat adhuc Laurus coronata, congestos inter nivium cumulos, frondescit inserta, flectitur in arcus, assurgit in colossos, in trophæa excrescit. Quid ampliùs? Diffluit in rivos lactis & sanguinis, ut niveo-purpureas sapientiæ baccas candido-purpureis Austriæ Philosophis propiner, funditur in succos, liquescit in remedia, desudat in balsamum, stillat in aquam vitæ. Inservit cæsa triumpho coronata Laurus CATHARINA, quando corpus truncum in latera, ramos in remos, comam in vela, in rudentes assamenta commodat, ut felicibus Austris ad portum Sapientiæ vestra naviget oneraria Neophilosophiæ: nisi malitis chartas pro carbasis, Porphyrij arborem pro malo navali, calamos pro remis, intellectûs acumen pro acu nauticâ, pro Saburrâ pulverem scholasticum, pro clavo clavam Philosophici Herculis clavini scientiarum exercitationem substituere, nè ad infamem à tot spectatis ruinis Arcadiæ pontem, naufragium incurratis. Hac sub Lauro coronatâ quiesce coronarum parens Austria, & imminentia barbari Martis fulmina (quæ Avernalis hærefeos tempestas in Austriæ minatur interitum) objectâ Lauro faciliùs eludes. O the most happy fecundity of the crowned Laurel CATHARINE, who, blessed with so many fruits, transmitted the fruitful shoots of her followers to posterity. You would call this Laurel the tree of life, whose immortal vigor in a mortal flower, still showing the green hope of fruitful flowers, having exited from the centuries, proceeds into the centuries, and will lose neither its beauty by the antiquity of time, nor its greenery by the turbine of hostile tempests, bargaining for immortal life through the very funerals of flowers: She allowed the glutton Maximinus a bite of her fruit, which was her blood, so that she might satisfy his voracious greed. She sends off the first shoots by the sword of Maximinus, so that through the cut-off germs of the Martyrs, she might be carried into the celestial gardens. Under this crowned Laurel, rest, Austria, parent of crowns, and you will more easily elude the impending lightnings of barbaric Mars (which the tempest of Avernian heresy threatens for the destruction of Austria) by interposing the Laurel. Live, Vienna, crowned with a new garland of victory; Live, Austria, always devoted to the crowned Laurel, and just as the Augusta Laurel vindicated Rhea, daughter of Numitor, King of the Albans, and her young son, Jupiter, from the implacable fury and insatiable greed of Saturn, know that you, with equal auspices, are to be liberated from the unstable glutton of kingdoms, who gapes at the Austrian Kingdoms, by the aid of the victorious Laurel. Indeed, this same most faithful guardian, placed before the August posts and doors of the most August House <note>(b) Ovid.</note>, will more happily break the three-forked weapons of thundering impiety. Fratris nomine sese cōmendat, quia illos vt fratres agnoscit. Deinde quia in re vtili illos fraternè admonet. *Nolo vos ignorare*. Ignoraturi videbantur, nisi Apostolus veras aperiret causas. Nam maleuoli data opera veritatem hîc occultabant, boni verò pauciores, & meliores audiri nō poterant, ideo ab Apostolo veritas fuit confirmanda, imò explicanda. Deinde narrationis statuit propositionem. Narraturus enim est de afflictione sua Asiatica. Locus est docilitatis. Nam qua de re hîc fit acturus ostendit. Perpessus est quidem alias infinitas persecutiones, sed non faciebant ad rem præsentem. Porrò quæ fuerit illa afflictio, nō satis constat. First, he establishes a <term>prodiēgēma</term> <gloss>preface/preliminary narration</gloss>, which is again accommodated for benevolence. *I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers*, i.e., of our affliction, which happened to us in Asia. He commends himself by the name of brother, because he acknowledges them as brothers. Next, because he admonishes them fraternally in a useful matter. *I do not want you to be ignorant*. They seemed destined to remain ignorant, unless the Apostle opened the true causes. For the malevolent were intentionally hiding the truth here, but the good were fewer, and the better could not be heard; therefore, the truth had to be confirmed, nay, explained, by the Apostle. Then he establishes the proposition of the narration. For he is about to narrate his Asian affliction. This is the place of docility. For he shows what matter he is going to act upon here. He had indeed suffered other infinite persecutions, but they did not pertain to the present matter. Furthermore, what that affliction was is not sufficiently certain. There are those who think it is the one in Acts 19, which was excited at Ephesus by Demetrius, but it is possible that it was some other much greater one, which was not written down by Luke.

II The narration itself concerning the magnitude of the affliction connects the parts through <term>aitiologian</term> <gloss>a causal account</gloss> (<term>hoti kath' hyperbolēn</term> <gloss>because beyond measure</gloss>). The magnitude makes for an excuse, which consists of three members. First, *I was burdened beyond strength*. There is a metaphor in the word <term>ebarēthēmen</term> <gloss>we were burdened</gloss>. For those are said to be burdened upon whom a greater weight is imposed, as if you were to impose a burden upon a boy that was meant for robust men. From this, therefore, he takes his excuse: The affliction was unequal to my strength, therefore I should not be accused.

Adiectiua tria, Anniculus, Ridiculus, uernaculus: anniculus puer, annicula puella, anniculum iumentum, hoc est unius anni: sicut Bimus, ma, mum, id est duorum annorum. Trimus, trima, trimum, id est trium annorum. Quadrimus, quadrima, quadrimum, id est quatuor annorum, et non amplius: nec de animalibus modo, sed de inanimatis, ut anniculum uinum, bimum oleum. De pueris tamen magis loquimur per diminutionem, bimulus, trimulus, quadrimulus, quia intra hos annos adhuc parui sunt. Similiter de his, in quibus haec ratio habet locum, ut anniculus equus, bimus aries, trimus porcus, quadrimum uinum, bimulus puer, trimula puella. Dissimiliter in quibus haec ratio locum non habet. Est etiam saepe neutrum, significatque plerunque sermonem risus potius, quam derisus excitantem. uernaculus, uernacula, uernaculum, quod est domi nostrae, uel in nostra patria natum, ut lingua uernacula, quod uulgo dicunt lingua materna: dictum est a uerna, qui est seruus domi nostrae natus, id est ex nostra ancilla. translation:
### Concerning diminutive nouns. Chapter V.

Diminutive nouns ending in such a sound as *pisciculus* <gloss>little fish</gloss>, if they are rightly formed, are true diminutives, such as *Pisciculus*, *vermiculus* <gloss>little worm</gloss>, *Passerculus* <gloss>little sparrow</gloss>, *Fraterculus* <gloss>little brother</gloss>, *Securicula* <gloss>little axe</gloss>, *Lucubratiuncula* <gloss>short period of work by candlelight</gloss>, *virguncula* <gloss>little maiden</gloss>, *Sororcula* <gloss>little sister</gloss>, *Munusculum* <gloss>little gift</gloss>, *Corpusculum* <gloss>little body</gloss>, *Mendaciunculum* <gloss>little lie</gloss>, *plusculum* <gloss>a little more</gloss>. If they are not rightly formed, they are not diminutives. *Auunculus* <gloss>uncle</gloss>, *Cuniculus* <gloss>rabbit/mine</gloss>, *Musculus* <gloss>muscle</gloss> (when it is not a small mouse), *Pediculus* <gloss>louse</gloss>, or (as others wish) *pedunculus* <gloss>peduncle</gloss>: and with a long penult, *cuculus* <gloss>cuckoo</gloss>. *Cicercula* <gloss>vetch</gloss> is the name of a legume. *Nouacula* <gloss>razor</gloss> is a shaving knife. *Lenticula* <gloss>lentil/small vessel</gloss> is a kind of small vessel: other masculine or feminine nouns do not occur. Servius, however, on Donatus says: *acus* <gloss>needle</gloss>, *acicula* <gloss>little needle/pin</gloss>. For *acus* is said of that which is used to mend clothes. *Acicula* is what women use for the ornament of the hair. Three adjectives: *Anniculus* <gloss>one year old</gloss>, *Ridiculus* <gloss>ridiculous</gloss>, *uernaculus* <gloss>vernacular/native</gloss>; *anniculus puer* <gloss>a boy of one year</gloss>, *annicula puella* <gloss>a girl of one year</gloss>, *anniculum iumentum* <gloss>a beast of one year</gloss>, that is, of one year: just as *Bimus, -ma, -mum*, that is, of two years. *Trimus, -ma, -mum*, that is, of three years. *Quadrimus, -ma, -mum*, that is, of four years, and no more: and this not only of animals, but of inanimate things, as *anniculum uinum* <gloss>one-year-old wine</gloss>, *bimum oleum* <gloss>two-year-old oil</gloss>. We speak of children, however, more through diminution: *bimulus*, *trimulus*, *quadrimulus*, because within these years they are still small. Similarly for those in which this reasoning holds place, such as *anniculus equus* <gloss>one-year-old horse</gloss>, *bimus aries* <gloss>two-year-old ram</gloss>, *trimus porcus* <gloss>three-year-old pig</gloss>, *quadrimum uinum* <gloss>four-year-old wine</gloss>, *bimulus puer* <gloss>young two-year-old boy</gloss>, *trimula puella* <gloss>young three-year-old girl</gloss>. Dissimilarly in those in which this reasoning has no place. *Ridiculus homo* <gloss>a ridiculous man</gloss>, *ridicula res* <gloss>a ridiculous thing</gloss>, *ridiculum caput* <gloss>a ridiculous person</gloss>, that is, to be laughed at. It is also often neuter, and generally signifies speech exciting laughter rather than ridicule. *Vernaculus, -la, -lum* is that which is born in our house or in our native land, such as *lingua uernacula* <gloss>vernacular language</gloss>, which common people call the mother tongue: it is said from *uerna*, which is a slave born in our house, that is, from our maid. Furthermore, there are many neuters, such as *umbraculum* <gloss>shady place</gloss>, *Tabernaculum* <gloss>tent</gloss>, *spectaculum* <gloss>spectacle</gloss>, *Habitaculum* <gloss>dwelling</gloss>, *Coenaculum* <gloss>dining room</gloss>, *Crepusculum* <gloss>twilight</gloss>, *Germiculum* for *germen* <gloss>bud</gloss>, *Crepitaculum* <gloss>rattle</gloss>, *Vinculum* <gloss>bond/chain</gloss>, *Amiculum* for a kind of clothing or garment, almost a cloak. *Curriculum* <gloss>course/running track</gloss> for a course, and for the place in which the competition of running is exercised, and sometimes also for a chariot, as Curtius in the eighth book: *The horses were thrown into confusion, casting them down not only into pits and marshes but even into the river’s courses <term>curricula</term>.* *Cubiculum* <gloss>bedroom</gloss>, which certainly does not come from *cubile* <gloss>bed</gloss>, since within a *cubiculum* there is a *cubile*, and its diminutive would be *cubicululum*. *Puluis* <gloss>dust</gloss> forms a diminutive both in meaning and in legitimate formation, but it changes gender according to Jerome, as *uile puluisculum* <gloss>vile little dust</gloss>: Apuleius, however, placed it in the masculine in one of his poems, of which he makes mention in his *Apology on Magic*: *I sent (as you asked) the refinements of teeth, the glosses of the mouth, / From Arabian fruits a thin, white, noble little dust <term>puluisculum</term>, / The smoother of the swollen gum, the weeder of yesterday's remains, / So that no foul stain of filth may be seen, / If by chance you smile with tightened lips.* *Conuentus* <gloss>assembly</gloss> also forms *conuenticulum* <gloss>little meeting place</gloss>.

the length and width of the measure you hold, multiply them by themselves, and you will have the feet or the area of the measure whose sides you multiplied; by which, if you divide the feet of the surface to be divided, the quotient will show the sought amount. Thus, the <term>iugera</term> <gloss>acres</gloss> of the first mountain will be 18, and 1600 feet over. The <term>iugera</term> of the second mountain will be 24, and 88,000 feet over. The <term>iugera</term> of the third mountain will be 21, and 6400 feet. Let these things be said concerning the measurement of surfaces; now we must come to the dimension of bodies.

->Measurement of the thickness or solidity of a sphere.<-

The measurement of a body seeks the solidities and thicknesses of bodies, such as how many feet the magnitude of the body contains. So that you may attain some knowledge of this, I shall set forth the method of measuring or the <term>praxis</term> <gloss>practical application</gloss> of certain bodies, and first indeed, that of a sphere. Therefore, if you wish to investigate the solidity of a sphere, you should multiply its diameter cubically (that is, multiply it by itself once in a square, and multiply the product again by the diameter). This cube exceeds the thickness of the sphere. However, with the excess removed, the solidity of the sphere is left. Furthermore, the excess will be revealed by this way: Divide the cube by 12, and multiply the product by 10, and you will have the sought excess. Or, multiply the diameter cubically, and multiply the product by 11, and the 21st part of the whole sum gives the solidity of the sphere. Thus, the excess multiplied by 11 will also give the same. For example, let there be a sphere whose diameter is 7. The cube will be 343, the excess 163 and one third part, and the thickness of the sphere 179 and two thirds.

fred. ad Rubricam Codex de Advocatis lex 1. littera g.
Quare autem Advocati dicantur **Togati** & **Scholastici** id si quis scire desideret adeat *Rittershusius* qui ad *Novellas* pagina 9. capitulo 8. numero 8. & sequuntur ex *Casaubono* ad *Capitolinum* posterius elegantius declarat ostendendo indici Scholasticos quia in Scholis fictis litibus & declamationibus quas *meletas* & meditationes appellabant se exercere soliti sunt. Advocare autem quod sicut diximus, officium hic denotat sumitur saepissime active ut in lex 18. *Digesta Rem ratam haberi* vide *Bachovius* ad τὰ πρῶτα titulus de Postulatione numero 1. pagina mea 742.

§. 10. Et sunt hi nihil aliud quam personae publicae quae litigantibus in judicio adsistunt consilio causam adjuvando vel legitime & recte proponendo deducendoque vide lex 6. §. 1. Codex de Postulatione lex 11. §. 1. Codex de Advocatis lege *Bachovius* ad τὰ πρῶτα titulus de Postulatione numero 1. *Seneca de brevitate vitae* capitulo 2. Dominus *Georgius Adam Struvius Exercitatio* 7. ad *Digesta* pagina 1. thesi 3. ex quo apparet qui alias dicuntur **Auscultantes**, ut in **Flandria** passim, proprie non esse Advocatos. Utpote cum illi nullas partium causas defendant, neutri partium serviant, nihil in judiciis orent, sed propterea saltem assumantur ut post adeptam juris scientiam stylum judicii addiscant, & procedendi modum observent, vide *Damhouderius Praxis rerum Civilium* capitulo 96. numero 2.

<column-break/>

§. 11. **Dicimus in Iudicio.** Et recte: non modo si judiciorum ordinem solemnem ante sublatas per Constantinum Imperatorem formulas respiciamus, sed & imprimis si rem secundum Dicasteria nostra examinemus. Iure enim Civili quamvis Postulatio seu Advocatio videatur pertinere ad jus, seu, ut apertius loquamur, ad ea judicia quae coram Magistratu superiori instituuntur argumentum lex 4. §. 8. *Digesta de damno infecto* verbi gratia Praetore vide lex 1. principium *Digesta de Postulatione* liquet tamen alios textus conjungentibus non minus recte quoque apud Magistratum inferiorem postulari vide Dominus *Henricus Hahnius* ad *Wesenbecium* titulus de Postulatione numero 2. pagina mea 439. quod & contra eundem vel per Senatusconsultum vel per Interpretationem prudentum ad judicem quoque Pedaneum pertinuisse arbitramur, propter lex 1. §. 6. versu item Senatusconsulto *Digesta de Postulatione* vide *Bachovius* ad τὰ πρῶτα titulus de Postulatione numero 1. pagina mea 743. *Gaddius de Verborum Significatione* ad lex 10. numero 2. & sequuntur *Brissonius* libro 5. *formularum populi Romani* quem adducit *Treutlerus* volumine 1. disputatio 8. thesi 1. littera B. **Hodiè Pedaneos Iudices** hoc est ad certam formulam adstrictos & nihil ultra nisi simplicem rei notionem sibi vindicantes non habemus vide lex 1. 2. Codex de Pedaneis judicibus *Paulus Christinaeus* volumine 2. decisionum 151. numero 1. 2. & sequitur *Groenewegen* ad titulus Codex qui pro sua iurisdictione iudices dare numero 1. & 2. sed propria omnibus competit Iurisdictio

translation:
to the rubric of the Code <note>original: "Codex"</note> on Advocates, law 1, letter g.
If anyone desires to know why advocates are called **Togati** <gloss>wearing the toga</gloss> and **Scholastici** <gloss>scholastics</gloss>, let him approach *Rittershusius*, who, at page 9, chapter 8, number 8 and following of his commentary on the *Novellae* <gloss>New Constitutions</gloss>, declares it more elegantly from *Casaubon* on the *Capitolinus* <note>referring to an author of the Historia Augusta</note>, showing they are called scholastics because they were accustomed to exercise themselves in the schools with mock disputes and declamations, which they called *meletas* <gloss>exercises/practice pieces</gloss> and meditations. Moreover, "to advocate" <term>advocare</term>, which as we said denotes the office here, is most often taken actively, as in law 18, *Digest* on "ratification of acts." See *Bachovius* on the *ta prota* <gloss>first things</gloss>, title on Postulation, number 1, page 742 of my copy.

§. 10. And these are nothing other than public persons who assist those litigating in court by helping the cause with counsel or by legally and correctly proposing and presenting it. See law 6, §. 1, Code on Postulation; law 11, §. 1, Code on Advocates; read *Bachovius* on *ta prota*, title on Postulation, number 1; *Seneca, On the Brevity of Life*, chapter 2; Lord *Georgius Adam Struvius*, Exercise 7 on the *Digest*, page 1, thesis 3. From this it appears that those who are otherwise called **Auscultantes** <gloss>listeners/auditors</gloss>, as in **Flanders** in many places, are not properly advocates. For they defend none of the parties' causes, serve neither party, and plead nothing in court; they are assumed only so that, after obtaining a knowledge of law, they may learn the style of the court and observe the manner of proceeding. See *Damhouderius, Practice of Civil Matters*, chapter 96, number 2.

<column-break/>

§. 11. **We say: in Court.** And correctly so: not only if we look at the solemn order of courts before the formulas were abolished by the Emperor Constantine, but also especially if we examine the matter according to our own courts <term>Dicasteria</term> <gloss>tribunals/courts</gloss>. For by Civil Law, although postulation or advocacy seems to pertain to the law—or, to speak more openly, to those trials that are instituted before a superior magistrate (argument from law 4, §. 8, *Digest* on "damage not yet done," for example, the Praetor; see law 1, the beginning of *Digest* on Postulation)—it is nevertheless clear from combining other texts that it is no less correctly petitioned before an inferior magistrate. See Lord *Henricus Hahnius* on *Wesenbecius*, title on Postulation, number 2, page 439 of my copy. We also judge that this pertains to the <term>pedaneous</term> <gloss>inferior/lower</gloss> judge, either by <term>Senatusconsultum</term> <gloss>decree of the senate</gloss> or by the interpretation of the learned, because of law 1, §. 6, at the verse "likewise by Senate decree," *Digest* on Postulation. See *Bachovius* on *ta prota*, title on Postulation, number 1, page 743 of my copy; *Gaddius, On the Signification of Words*, on law 10, number 2 and following; *Brissonius*, book 5 of *The Formulas of the Roman People*, whom *Treutlerus* cites in volume 1, disputation 8, thesis 1, letter B. **Today we do not have Pedaneous Judges** <gloss>inferior judges tied to a formula</gloss>, that is, judges restricted to a certain formula and claiming nothing for themselves beyond a simple notion of the matter. See law 1, 2, Code on Pedaneous Judges; *Paulus Christinaeus*, volume 2, decision 151, numbers 1 and 2; and *Groenewegen* on the title of the Code "Which judges for their own jurisdiction," numbers 1 and 2. But jurisdiction itself belongs to all.
